But a long time ago, I took an intro to Evelyn Woods speed reading (remember them?) and the key they said was to keep your eyes moving steadily across each line instead of jumping from phrase to phrase as is normally done.  They did it with using your finger to move steadily across each line to get the words in faster.  I find that a pain.  But instead, I have a plain bookmark which I put under each line at a slight angle down to the left so as I slide it down the page, more words appear and it helps keep me reading more quickly. title: Cluttered to Chic: Transforming a Home’s Heart into a Masterpiece | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "snug-nest-designs-pfvwau-pf~256404672", "author_name": "Snug Nest Designs", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/snug-nest-designs-pfvwau-pf~256404672", "date": "2025-02-01", "text": "Every project begins with a deeper understanding of our clients\u2014beyond just their needs and requirements. By uncovering their aspirations and motivations, we tap into the heart of why they seek a renovation. Often, our clients haven\u2019t fully identified the root of their challenges, and this is where our expertise truly shines. We guide them in clarifying their vision and unlocking the full potential of their space. In this project, we\u2019ll take you through our process, illustrating how thoughtful design can elevate and transform the way we live every day. Before  After  How It Started Our clients initially sought to refresh their bar area, but during our on-site consultation, we uncovered a broader opportunity to enhance their home. As we delved deeper into their needs and lifestyle, the true potential of their space began to unfold. What started as a simple update blossomed into a holistic transformation, where form and function harmonized to create a space that not only looks stunning but also perfectly mirrors their unique way of life. Cocktail Corner To Study Nook The protruding bar counter occupied valuable space in the living room, disrupting the natural flow and compromising the TV wall\u2019s functionality. It obstructed the room\u2019s circulation, creating an imbalanced feel. Meanwhile, the narrow 1.1-meter space behind the counter remained largely underused\u2014an untapped opportunity to reimagine it into something both functional and dynamic.   After gaining a clear understanding of their need for a functional workspace, we proposed removing the bar to open up space for a functional study nook, transforming an underutilized area into a purposeful retreat. To maintain a light and airy feel, a floating desk and shelf were installed to maximize the tight space. Pin boards and task lighting were added to enhance functionality. Slatted paneling on the wall introduced texture, while subtle touches of brown in the artwork and chairs brought warmth and character to the space.     Living Room Glow-Up The spacious 5m x 5m living room held a wealth of untapped potential. Despite its generous proportions, the room felt more confined than it truly was, largely due to the heavy, cumbersome furniture and a disjointed layout. The previous arrangement obstructed the natural flow, with circulation paths cutting through the seating area, disrupting the room's harmony. Additionally, the abundance of natural light from the large windows went unappreciated, as poor lighting choices left the space feeling dim and uninspired. The lack of visual cohesion further diminished the room\u2019s character and identity. The absence of a unified color scheme\u2014walls painted in various hues and furniture in an eclectic mix of dark and bright tones\u2014created an imbalance that prevented the room from feeling whole and inviting.   The first step in transforming the living room was decluttering the space and updating the overall color scheme to a sophisticated and contemporary neutral palette with warm undertones. The walls, ceiling, and skirting boards were all painted in the soft natural white tone, creating a seamless, light-reflecting backdrop. Reimagining the furniture layout was a complete game changer. By bringing the seating area forward, we reshaped the room's entire atmosphere. This shift not only made the space feel more expansive by creating unobstructed pathways around the seating area, it also optimized the flow of natural light. To further enhance this, we introduced sheer curtains, allowing light to flood the room while maintaining a soft, airy ambiance.   We recommended replacing the sofa and chairs with lighter, more streamlined pieces, embracing soft, curved shapes that fostered an inviting and elegant atmosphere. The choice of swivel chairs added both functionality and flexibility, allowing the seating area to adapt with minimal effort. With the clients\u2019 love for reading in mind, we relocated the fish tank and corner shelves to carve out a cozy reading nook in the corner. A rocking chair, chosen for its playful yet comfortable design, became a charming focal point. To further enhance the nook's functionality, we installed floating shelves for easy access to books, while an elegant arc floor lamp provided task lighting. A photo wall was added to showcase cherished family moments, providing a warm and inviting backdrop to the reading nook.   Given that the clients have a dog, we recommended replacing the flooring with a lighter shade of hybrid wood, ensuring easy maintenance without compromising style. Textures were introduced through the swivel lounge chairs, rug, and carefully placed plants, adding depth and visual interest. To bring the room together and infuse character, we selected a statement pendant light that offers both form and function. From TV wall to Feature Wall The old TV unit felt outdated and was visually disproportionate to the expansive 3m wall it sat against, largely due to the bar counter that dominated much of the TV wall. This design oversight turned the TV into an afterthought.   We envisioned transforming the TV wall into the centerpiece of the living room. To achieve this, we custom-built the TV unit from the ground up, carefully maximizing the length of the 3-meter wall. To create a warm, inviting atmosphere, we selected rich timber wall paneling, complemented by a striking marble stone accent that introduces a sophisticated contrast. Soft ambient lighting was incorporated to highlight the natural beauty of the timber and add depth, bringing the wall to life. To preserve the room's contemporary aesthetic, we kept accessories minimal, allowing the TV wall to command attention as the room\u2019s focal point.   Dining Room Refresh The generously sized 4m x 4m dining area felt just as confined as the living room, with heavy, dark-colored furniture that further compressed the space. An overabundance of small items\u2014accumulated over the years on the console table and shelves\u2014contributed to the visual clutter. The lighting was also insufficient: the pendant light failed to provide adequate illumination, and the natural light from the glass doors was under-utilised, leaving the room feeling dim and poorly lit.   To restore balance, we replaced the heavy chairs with lighter-toned wingback chairs that complemented the bold presence of the concrete dining table. These modern, lightweight chairs helped create visual continuity between the living and dining areas. A sleek, modern buffet table was also added, seamlessly integrating with the other furnishings. To maximize natural light, sheer curtains were installed, allowing sunlight to flow freely into the room. Above the buffet, a round, contemporary mirror was placed to reflect and amplify the light, enhancing the room\u2019s soft, airy ambiance. A multi-light pendant introduced visual interest and character. To complete the cozy, welcoming atmosphere, we carefully selected accessories like natural stoneware and a plush, high-pile rug.     From Vision to Reality: What Our Client Says! \"After years of agonizing over what to do to remove a dated bar in our loungeroom area we engaged Srishti from Snug Nest Designs to look at the space with creative and unbiased eyes.  We gave her the freedom to look at the whole living space as a blank canvas. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~564423447", "author_name": "The KEEPING ROOM", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~564423447", "date": "2025-02-16", "text": "The most difficult repair there is on a piece of wood furniture a horizontal table top with a small blemish.  They are virtually impossible to repair without refinishing the entire top which includes sanding the old finish off entirely (or using a scraper, etc).  I would not attempt to fix it, just live with it.  There is a very high chance you will make it worse, not better.  Dark woods are easier to repair as you can bring in color agents and adjust - on light tables such as yours I would not even attempt it.  Even if you get a color blend, you will never match the sheen and have a low or high spot.  Never bring heat to a wood repair, that can reflow the existing finish and if that happens you will, for sure, have a total top refinish project.  If tomato soup stained that table, then there is little to no protective finish on it, it may just have oil and wax. I'm trying to figure out a good height that will fit stools, and I would like it at a comfortable level so the sink can be on the other side. We do not want to do two separate heights for a lower and higher island. Did you also make the cabinets on the wall the same height as the island?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ba2151130088a120_8266-w500-h333-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "plush-design-interiors-pfvwau-pf~1921601306", "author_name": "Plush Design Interiors", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-designers-and-decorators/plush-design-interiors-pfvwau-pf~1921601306", "date": "2025-02-03", "text": "Hi Jane, a typical bench height is 900mm but it depends on how tall you are. We design kitchens with bench tops between 900mm and 930mm high. The height of the bar stools then depend on the depth of your kitchen countertop. Always measure - bar stools may be a slightly different height from kitchen stools. I would make the countertops all the same height. For upper cabinets, they are not as deep as the countertop - a countertop may be 600mm - 700mm deep (typically) whereas overhead cupboards shouldn't be more than around 350mm deep. And we put open shelves or overheads at least 400mm above the countertop height - depends on how tall you are. Hope that helps. Cheers, Penelope", "images": []}}

title: A kind of morbid estate planning topic | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "3katz4me", "author_name": "3katz4me", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3katz4me", "date": "2025-02-03", "text": "So we met with a new attorney in our new state to rework our estate plan.  We haven't updated it in 19 years and the friends ID'd to manage our affairs are our age and now 19 years older than when we chose them. Since we have no kids and no other relatives we'd want to be in charge (or burden with all our stuff in two different states) we are revamping the whole thing to be handled by a professional trustee (attorney).  Fortunately we got a great referral from another kid-less couple we met here. So it's all pretty straightforward but for the three cats.  The current plan is that our estate makes a sizeable contribution to a specified feline rescue organization and they find a home for our cats.  Ideally I'd like a trusted cat-loving friend to take them but that just isn't going to happen.  I'm not sure if the attorney or DH mentioned it first but the attorney has had some clients who decide the pet(s) will get the kevorkian treatment when the people die.  The idea being that life after their people die will be so traumatic and future care so questionable that they don't want their pets to suffer through that. We are those people whose pets are their \"children\".  So we'd be turning the \"kids\" over to some orphanage where they'd likely be in a cage for at least a while until foster and/or adoptive parents could be found.  Adult cats...hmmm.....how many unwanted adult cats are out there in shelters and foster groups?   And hmmm.....just how kind and loving is that foster/adoptive home going to be? Though I'd never, ever considered kevorkian to be an estate planning solution I'm now actually considering it.  Our last kitty to pass on did so with Lap of Love and it was the most peaceful, loving experience we've ever had with that.  If we're blessed, at least one of us will live into our mid-80s with our physical and mental faculties intact and there won't be a need for such a thing (as long as I don't get any more cats). title: Upgrade Your Living Room with These Blind Ideas | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "external-venetian-blindssure-shade-pfvwau-pf~441488278", "author_name": "External Venetian Blinds:Sure Shade", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/window-treatments/external-venetian-blindssure-shade-pfvwau-pf~441488278", "date": "2025-02-04", "text": "When it comes to home decor, one of the most important elements often overlooked is the choice of blinds. A simple change to your window coverings can have a dramatic impact on the overall look and feel of a room. For those looking to elevate their living room\u2019s design, the addition of high-quality blinds is an excellent solution. Among the various types of window coverings, External Venetian Blinds stand out as an ideal choice, offering not only aesthetic appeal but also practical benefits. In this article, we\u2019ll explore how you can upgrade your living room with stylish and functional blind ideas, focusing on the advantages of External Venetian Blinds, and why Sure Shade is your go-to brand for these premium window solutions. 1. Why Choose External Venetian Blinds? External Venetian Blinds have long been favored by homeowners and interior designers alike for their versatility and sleek design. They are particularly popular for living rooms, as they help create a comfortable atmosphere while enhancing the overall aesthetic of the space. Here's why these blinds are an excellent choice for your living room: Superior Light Control One of the biggest advantages of External Venetian Blinds is their ability to control the amount of natural light entering a room. They allow you to adjust the angle of the slats, giving you complete control over how much light filters into your living room. Whether you prefer a bright, sunlit space or a more subdued, cozy atmosphere, these blinds offer flexibility. The external positioning of these blinds also helps reduce glare and heat from direct sunlight, keeping your living room comfortable all year round. Energy Efficiency In addition to light control, External Venetian Blinds help improve the energy efficiency of your living room. They act as an extra layer of insulation, reducing the amount of heat that enters your home during the summer months and helping to retain warmth in the winter. This insulation can lower your energy bills, making them an eco-friendly and cost-effective choice. Enhanced Privacy and Protection External Venetian Blinds are also designed to provide better privacy compared to their internal counterparts. Since they are positioned on the exterior of your windows, they block the view from outside while still allowing you to enjoy the outside scenery. These blinds also offer protection against UV rays, preventing your furniture and artwork from fading due to prolonged sun exposure. 2. Choosing the Right Style for Your Living Room Now that you understand the benefits of External Venetian Blinds, the next step is to choose the right style to complement your living room's design. Sure Shade offers a wide range of styles and finishes to suit various tastes and interior themes. Classic Aluminum Blinds If you\u2019re looking for a sleek and modern design, classic aluminum Venetian Blinds are the perfect option. Available in various colors and finishes, they add a contemporary touch to your living room. Aluminum blinds are durable, lightweight, and easy to maintain, making them an ideal choice for high-traffic areas. Wooden Venetian Blinds For those who prefer a more natural, warm aesthetic, wooden Venetian Blinds are an excellent choice. These blinds bring a touch of elegance to your living room, adding texture and depth to the space. Wooden blinds also pair well with a variety of furniture styles, from rustic to contemporary, making them a versatile option for any design scheme. Modern Faux Wood Blinds Faux wood blinds are an affordable alternative to traditional wooden blinds, offering the same stylish appearance without the higher price tag. These blinds are made from composite materials, making them durable, moisture-resistant, and easy to clean. Faux wood External Venetian Blinds are perfect for those seeking the look of wood without the upkeep. 3. Maximizing the Impact of Your Living Room\u2019s Design When integrating External Venetian Blinds into your living room, it\u2019s important to consider how they can enhance the overall decor. Here are some ideas on how to maximize the impact of these blinds: Coordinate with Your Color Scheme The color of your External Venetian Blinds should complement the existing color scheme of your living room. Lighter colors, such as white or beige, can make the space feel more open and airy, while darker tones like charcoal or navy blue add sophistication and drama. Sure Shade offers a variety of colors, so you can easily match the blinds to your furniture, walls, and accents. Layer with Curtains or Drapes For an added layer of texture and warmth, consider layering your Venetian Blinds with curtains or drapes. This combination works particularly well in living rooms that need extra softness or a more luxurious feel. Choose curtains that match your blinds\u2019 color or opt for contrasting hues to create a bold statement. Play with Different Textures Blinds are not just about functionality \u2013 they also contribute to the texture of your living room. The sleek, smooth finish of Venetian Blinds pairs beautifully with plush sofas, textured rugs, and woven baskets. By mixing different textures in your living room, you create a visually appealing and dynamic space that feels cozy and inviting. Add Decorative Elements To make your living room feel more personalized, consider adding decorative elements around your External Venetian Blinds. This could include placing indoor plants, artwork, or sculptures near the windows. These additions can draw attention to the blinds while enhancing the overall decor of your living room. 4. Maintenance Tips for Long-Lasting Style One of the main reasons why External Venetian Blinds are such a great investment is their durability. However, like any home feature, they require some basic maintenance to keep them looking their best. Here are a few tips to ensure your blinds continue to enhance your living room for years to come: Regular Cleaning To keep your External Venetian Blinds looking pristine, it\u2019s important to clean them regularly. Dust and dirt can accumulate on the slats, so use a microfiber cloth or a soft duster to wipe them down. If your blinds are particularly dirty, you can use a mild detergent solution and a sponge to give them a more thorough clean. title: Brick Damage / Discoloration on 10 year old Home | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kson", "author_name": "kson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kson", "date": "2025-02-05", "text": "We noticed this brick damage / discoloration on a 10 year old home we placed an offer on. Inspector will look at it when he comes tomorrow but would love others advice on what is causing this and extent of the potential damage. Appears that they had ivy growing in this spot and sprinklers placed right up against the house causing some level of mold. This is also next to the daylight windows of a finished basement. No obvious signs of water damage in interior. But could there be trapped water in the bricks making its way inside or foundation issues?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/be826b2c07a32f44_7719-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/efa249da07a32f45_7720-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1fb27e3007a32f46_7720-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "outpaientzero", "author_name": "outpaientzero", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/outpaientzero", "date": "2025-02-05", "text": "There are a few reasons the efflorescence can get so bad on a 10 year old brick walls, and build quality  is one.  I rarely see efflorescence on 100 year old brick walls this bad so suspect the walls on that house used poor quality mortar, old mortar or wrong mixing ratios.  If the mortar can be scraped off with a fingernail is was old or cheap.  Mortar will go bad just sitting in the bags and seen it go bad in less than a year. The bricks could be low quality soft bricks with high salt content (All bricks have hardness ratings).  A butter knife can easily rub off brick material on cheap soft bricks.  I suspect cheap materials because the efflorescence is running so high up the walls and not normal at all. Because the knowledge level and quality of home inspectors are so low I'd pay a expert in the field to take a look.  You don't want to buy a house with bad mortar unless you're willing to pay 10's of thousands to have a mason grind out 3/4-1 inch of mortar and apply new mortar. Another problem is the algae growing on the wall, the brick is very damp to do this.  I noticed the soil level is above the bottom bricks.  Bricks are porous and will wick up moisture from the ground, and the bottom brick row shouldn't be below ground level.  In fact the bottom row should have weep holes to allow moisture to weep out from behind the bricks, I don't see any, or they are buried below the ground, or they didn't put weep holes in.  Google weep holes in brick walls to see what I'm talking about. Brick walls aren't in contact with the wall behind them, they are actually about an inch away from the wall and held off with tabs nailed to the wall and then attached between rows of brick.  On the wall behind the bricks is a layer of waterproofing material like tar paper or equivalent.  The cavity between the bricks and wall is deliberately made along with the weep holes to channel moisture down the back of the bricks and out.  I don't know what's going on for sure so do not hesitate bringing in a professional mason to evaluate the problem.", "images": []}}

The rain will slide onto the grass area and a large grate. My question is: We are thinking of laying Ekodeck that will extended to under the pergola area (onto the other lighter grey concrete). I was thinking an option can be to make a few boards shorter to create two rectangular spaces and plant some palms in them which will also act as more drainage for rain. main_question: {"author_id": "jyl-gw", "author_name": "John Liu", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jyl-gw", "date": "2025-02-06", "text": "Walk in pantries  get  discussed  a  lot.  I  thought,  why  not  airtime  for  the  alternative of  pantry cabinets? A  pantry  cabinet,  to me, is i) a built-in cabinet  ii) away  from  the  kitchen  core work  triangle  (ice-water-stone-fire), iii) designed  to  hold  a  large   volume of  things both  large  and  small,  that  may be needed  every  day  or every  week  but  not  every  minute or every hour, with  nothing  hidden or lost. It  is  an  alternative to  a  walk in  pantry  and  to a free-standing piece  like a hutch. The  reason  I natter  on  about  pantry  cabinets is  that  they  are  often  more  efficient and  effective  than  the  alternatives. Unlike a walk-in pantry,  the  pantry  cabinet  does not need  to  hold a person  or two people, and  give them  room to bend over, squat, turn around.    The   volume  not  used  to  hold  a human body can be  used to  hold  pasta  and  stockpots.   This  advantage  fades if  you  do,  indeed,  want to  hold bodies, so discerning serial killers endorse walk-in pantries  and  I  certainly  won\u2019t  argue with them. Unlike a free-standing piece,  the  pantry  cabinet  can be sized  exactly to the  space  available, is  securely  anchored  to the  wall  without  tipping  issues, and  can  be  customized for  the  user\u2019s  needs  without  hiring a custom furniture maker  who  are  more  expensive than  custom cabinet makers.  Lots.  More.  Expensive. These virtues allow a pantry  cabinet to  be placed  where  there is   not  enough  space  for  a walk-in pantry  and  not the  right  shape/size of  space  for  grandma\u2019s baking hutch.  A nook, a corner,  even  a passageway,  the  empty  space  where  a laundry chute or  water  heater  used to  be. If  you  are  going to  build  or  have  built a pantry cabinet, I  recommend  against  the  all-drawer  stack  that  we  use in  base  cabinets.   Instead, use doors  with  rollout shelves.  Yes,  this requires  three actions (open right door, open left door, pull out shelf)  instead of  one  (pull out drawer),  but  we\u2019ve stipulated  the  things  there are  needed  daily or weekly, not  every  five minutes.  Have  the  cabinet insides pre-drilled so  that  your  slides  can  be  easily re-positioned higher or lower.   When  you  switch to  a  different  brand of cooking sake  that  comes in  a taller bottle, just re-position  the  shelf.  Can\u2019t  do  that  with  drawers. A  pantry  cabinet  can  be  fitted with  electrical  outlets  to  become the  much-maligned  appliance  garage,  but  one that  isn\u2019t  taking up  counter  space.  Heat  and  steam-producing  appliances  shouldn\u2019t  be operated  in  there,  at least  not with  doors closed,  but  your  blender  and  mixer  are  fine.  Better yet if  their  shelf  pulls out to use them in the  open.  Better  again yet  if  your  cabinet maker  builds in  pullout workboards  to  put things on  as  you  use  the  mixer - or  simply  to  set  down grocery  bags. Have you built  pantry  cabinets  into  your  kitchen?  I would  like to  see people\u2019s  creative, useful, lovely, useful, cool, useful pantry cabinets.  From Ikea to full-zoot custom, all  are  appreciated!", "images": []}

title: Bathroom design for elderly | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "nadiagn", "author_name": "nadiagn", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nadiagn", "date": "2025-02-06", "text": "Hi there, my elderly parents are designing their new retirement (and forever) home. One area I am particularly concerned about is ensuring the bathroom layout will be suitable for them as they age. Can anyone share bathroom designs specially for older people and/or suggestions of what to be be mindful off. I've already considered things like ensuring zero threshold shower and a hand held shower  head - but Im struggling to get my head around the layout and room dimensions.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kendrahhendra", "author_name": "Kendrah", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kendrahhendra", "date": "2025-02-07", "text": "Researched this a lot for my parents and hired an OT / design specialist.  Here is what I learned. No pony wall or separate toilet area.  Grab bar on one wall and other side of toilet have enough space for a caregiver or helper if ever needed.  Should it come to needing a grab bar on that second wall, you can install one on the wall behind the toilet that folds down. Forget ADA compliant.  That is designed for public usage to accomodate the average person.  In a home you want to accomodate a specific person - your parents.  Mount things at a height that makes sense for their height, where their arm extends to when they reach out. Put blocking in the walls for lots of grab bars.  You don't have to install them now.  Just know where they are so they can be installed in the future. Don't get a grab bar that doubles as a towel rod.  Lots of falls happen from people grabbing those and the towel on the surface makes it not gripable.  Use strategically placed grab bars and towel hooks instead.  Never make a surface that can be grasped and leaned on that isn't totally safe to take weight. Have the door open out.  If they fall in the bathroom and the door opens in, they might be in front of the door and it makes it very hard to get into the bathroom to assist them. Height of sink, again, based on their height. Nice to have a lot of counterspace so they don't have to look down, lean down, twist around to get things from lower cabinets.  (Think head rush, off balance, leading to falls when you bend down and stand up.) Unless they have a specific disease where you know they will be in a wheelchair, it isn't not necessary to make this wheelchair accessible.  Only 4-7% of elders end up in a wheelchair. Place shower controls at arm reach height, again not bending.  Place a vertical grab bar near controls so they can hold the bar while adjusting the controls. Have lots of horizontal bars in the shower to hold on to while washing their body.  Don't make the shower too big.  It gets cold.  And they have to walk farther to on a wet surface to reach the bench and controls. Really nice to have a place to sit and dry off and a surface or hooks to put clothes on that they will wear for the day. Don't believe that mosaic tiles provide enough non-slip traction because of groutlines.  Get anti-slip rated tiles.", "images": []}}

title: What important product or service you liked has declined or vanished? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "elmerjfudd", "author_name": "Elmer J Fudd", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/elmerjfudd", "date": "2025-02-08", "text": "I'm not a Luddite. I look to most of the major changes in life (and technology) during my lifetime and see mostly massive significant changes for the better. Daily life today for most people is easier, more convenient, and with more possibilities readily accessible than was the case for how things were when I was a child and during much of my life. Improvements year by year, step by step. I like positive changes and am open to trying new things and new ways. My limited nostalgia relates only to good memories of people, not things. With one exception - I REALLY miss the time when the newspaper business in the US was thriving. I really miss the depth and content of stories and investigations that seemingly only newspapers had the time and people to produce. Folks whose daily routines included reading a newspaper were better informed than people are now and as a result were more literate. In addition to being better informed about real news, they were entertained and enlightened by human interest stories that opened a crack into some aspect of people, places or things going on in the area that without which, no one would have ever known about. The fun of reading out of town newspapers that were available at newsstands was another benefit, though that is available online in a few limited instances of those few good ones left standing. Every page of any decent newspaper had something to offer. Even the classified ads did. Part of what I see as the dumbing down of American society might have been different without the decline of the newspaper business. Thanks Craigslist, whose emergence doomed papers by taking away the major source of their revenue - classified ads. That's my contribution to this topic. What thoughts do you have?", "images": []}

title: PSA — ❄️for residents in snow areas — let’s share tips❄️ | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "petalique", "author_name": "petalique", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/petalique", "date": "2025-02-09", "text": "\u2744\ufe0f\u2603\ufe0f We are in New England, but a wide area beyond that will be dealing with snow and icy roads. Let\u2019s share some tips for winter weather with snow and ice. I will offer a few: \u2744\ufe0f Finish doing car errands way before snow and ice is expected. A lot of regions treat roadways with Magnesium Chloride ahead of expected precipitation. This stuff is extremely corrosive to metal and other automobile components. Even though you may wash your vehicle after a snow and ice storm, it is best to avoid getting any of this material on your car. It is often applied in brine form, but can remain on the roadways and in snowbanks after the storm is over. Magnesium chloride is much more corrosive that salt. \u2744\ufe0f After the storm, be careful when you are out and about. Plow drivers and other trucks and vehicles seem to blithely whiz through and across parking lots \u2014 at shopping centers, condo areas and town or city streets. Every year, people, including children are injured by cowboy drivers. Avoid walking across parking lots on in areas where snowbanks or darkness impede visibility. Get a small very bright LED and put it on flash blink mode. Communicate to others, elders, kids not to assume that drivers are paying attention and will see them. In the past month a 14 year old was hit and killed by a truck while he was walking across a parking lot. Laast week a woman was clearing snow of her car in her condo parking lot when a plow driver hit her and knocked her under his truck. Plowing snow is fun and plow drivers are eager to make as much income as they can and are sometime young and inexperienced. Be mindful. \u2744\ufe0f Remind children and other to avoid walking or playing beneath trees, the snow laden branches  can suddenly snap and crash down. A few years ago a young girl was home from school because of a snowstorm. She was playing outdoors, enjoying the snow when the branch of a tree crashed down upon her (fatally). We have large trees close to us and try to be mindful when going to the roadside mailbox in windy or snowy weather. It doesn\u2019t take a very large branch to injure of kill a person beneaht it when it falls. \u2744\ufe0f Of course, have a few things like batteries, flashlights and extra water on hand. Then relax and enjoy the snowfall. We also fill our suet and birdseed dispensers up the day before and day of any big storm.", "images": []}

title: PSA — ❄️for residents in snow areas — let’s share tips❄️ | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "petalique", "author_name": "petalique", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/petalique", "date": "2025-02-09", "text": "PSA \u2014 \u2744\ufe0ffor residents in snow areas \u2014 let\u2019s share tips\u2744\ufe0f petaliqueFebruary 8, 2025 \u2744\ufe0f\u2603\ufe0f We are in New England, but a wide area beyond that will be dealing with snow and icy roads. Let\u2019s share some tips for winter weather with snow and ice. I will offer a few: \u2744\ufe0f Finish doing car errands way before snow and ice is expected. A lot of regions treat roadways with Magnesium Chloride ahead of expected precipitation. This stuff is extremely corrosive to metal and other automobile components. Even though you may wash your vehicle after a snow and ice storm, it is best to avoid getting any of this material on your car. It is often applied in brine form, but can remain on the roadways and in snowbanks after the storm is over. Magnesium chloride is much more corrosive that salt. \u2744\ufe0f After the storm, be careful when you are out and about. Plow drivers and other trucks and vehicles seem to blithely whiz through and across parking lots \u2014 at shopping centers, condo areas and town or city streets. Every year, people, including children are injured by cowboy drivers. Avoid walking across parking lots on in areas where snowbanks or darkness impede visibility. Get a small very bright LED and put it on flash blink mode. Communicate to others, elders, kids not to assume that drivers are paying attention and will see them. In the past month a 14 year old was hit and killed by a truck while he was walking across a parking lot. Laast week a woman was clearing snow of her car in her condo parking lot when a plow driver hit her and knocked her under his truck. Plowing snow is fun and plow drivers are eager to make as much income as they can and are sometime young and inexperienced. Be mindful. \u2744\ufe0f Remind children and other to avoid walking or playing beneath trees, the snow laden branches can suddenly snap and crash down. A few years ago a young girl was home from school because of a snowstorm. She was playing outdoors, enjoying the snow when the branch of a tree crashed down upon her (fatally). We have large trees close to us and try to be mindful when going to the roadside mailbox in windy or snowy weather. It doesn\u2019t take a very large branch to injure of kill a person beneaht it when it falls. \u2744\ufe0f Of course, have a few things like batteries, flashlights and extra water on hand. Then relax and enjoy the snowfall. We also fill our suet and birdseed dispensers up the day before and day of any big storm. I could not cross post this from The Kitchen Table. Geez. main_question: {"author_id": "plllog", "author_name": "plllog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/plllog", "date": "2025-02-09", "text": "I'm not getting one!  Don't worry.  I have a fully equipped kitchen and I know how to cook.  From what I gather, the Thermomix is for people with limited kitchens and those who don't know how to cook.  I'd heard that the current model had really come into its own, however, and is available in the USA (even from Amazon--i.e., no longer in specialty shops, and I was curious.  There are also some knock offs which look way too much like the original).  I had some time to, um, \"waste\" today so watched Thermomix videos. So, as best as I understand, there's a boiling element, a four bladed knife that goes both directions, and a scale.  There are also accessories to make it do more, plus a \"cutter\", which is an additional purchase, which slices and grates like FP disks.  Oh, and a large touch screen which accesses tens of thousands of recipes, and a personal consultant.  I didn't get any real info about the consultant, but I infer it's supposed to be like calling your mom when you're young and don't understand what you're supposed to do (given a mom who cooks (well)). So, the 2.2 litre jar is where stuff happens.  The knife looks like a big fancy blender knife, and the base and knife disassemble for cleaning, etc.  It seems that the way the knife is made it can do Vita-mix style blending, food processor chopping, and in reverse using the dull side, knead dough.  There's an included plastic insert to whip cream or eggwhites. and a \"simmering basket\" which sits above the knife for steaming eggs, rice, veggies, etc., and which can be used as a colander or steamer basket.  There is also a big dish with a tray that sits in it and cover for the stack.  You can steam a whole meal in those without having to jam them into the basket.  I.e., basket is good for steaming rice or eggs, but make your fish and broccoli in the dish thing.  I guess it works. title: Buying home from an estate. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rnmomof2", "author_name": "RNmomof2 zone 5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rnmomof2", "date": "2025-02-09", "text": "There is a house in my neighborhood that we may be interested in buying.  The house is 35 years old and the original owners have passed away.  The house is of interested to either us or our DD to live in.  We have reached out to the attorney and will see the house this spring after an auction.  This couple has 2 children who do not want the house or any of the contents. Question-this house is dated inside.  It has wall paper in many rooms, odd paint colors on walls, original floors in many rooms.  Basically it needs some decor updating.  The landscape and trees were also butchered perhaps beyond repair last fall.  All of the neighbors are unsure if some of it will come back this spring. Using this info, how does one determine what to offer?  My DD has been working with a realtor, unsure if she would help with comps for a fee or to get her involved. We both have only been in the public areas of the house so this may be a nonissue when the entire house is seen.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jennifer-hogan285", "author_name": "Jennifer Hogan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jennifer-hogan285", "date": "2025-02-10", "text": "I think I understand.  The original owner passed away and you would like to buy the home so that your child can live close to you / in the same neighborhood. Assuming they are auctioning all the contents, then will have the house cleaned and put on the market or have it auctioned.   I know several \"kids\" who opted to have the house auctioned vs the typical selling process.  They didn't want the headaches and auction was the easy button. Two of my nieces bought homes in the past 3 years that were being sold by the children of the owner.  One the owner had passed away, the other the owner went to an Alzheimer Care facility. You need to be a bit more careful in this type of transaction because the disclosure will be fairly worthless.   If the kids didn't live in the house they can claim ignorance of past issues, so question after question is answered \"unknown\".   (Has the roof ever leaked?  unknown) If the seller was living in the home they would be required to answer yes or no and if they lied you can go to an attorney and make them pay for issues with the roof. One of my nieces bought 2 years ago and where she bought things were moving really fast.   Properties had multiple offers come in within a day or two of listing and most were giving a deadline to have your offer in within 3-4 days of listing and most were turning away offers with contingencies.   In my nieces case the realtor for the seller told my nieces agent that they would not allow an inspection.  The kids did not want to know if something was wrong because they would have to disclose it and it could lower the price.   We hired an inspector to walk through of the home and provide verbal feedback on anything he thought was a red flag.  He pointed out quite a few things we would not have noticed, but didn't find any big red flags. My other niece bought just a few months ago in a different city.   The market was not as hot and she had her offer accepted with an inspection as a contingency. Only you and the realtors in your area can determine how hot the market is in your neighborhood and what may or may not be accepted.   Since they are selling through their estate attorney, I would expect that they won't want an inspection.   If they allow an inspection and the sale falls through they would have to disclose any issues found in the inspection. Because you live in the neighborhood you may have a good idea of what issues have been experienced in the neighborhood.   Were the homes all built around the same time and built by the same builder?     Some neighborhoods are more standardized, some are all custom homes built over decades by different builders. Price is generally based on square footage and neighborhood with some allowance for the general condition of the property. You should be able to get comps run by any realtor or find them yourself online.   What has sold in the neighborhood in the past 6 months.   Sometimes you have to go to similar neighborhoods that are close by if their haven't been any sales or only 1 or 2 sales in your specific neighborhood. If they want a quick sale without paying realtor commissions and your offer is reasonable they may not want to bother with going on the market.", "images": []}}

title: How to Use a Chin-Up Dip Station | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "relife-sports-pfvwus-pf~944447487", "author_name": "Relife sports", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/home-stagers/relife-sports-pfvwus-pf~944447487", "date": "2025-02-11", "text": "A home gym chin-up dip station is an excellent piece of equipment for targeting your upper body, especially your back, arms, chest, and shoulders. It typically combines both chin-up bars and dip bars into one compact unit, making it a versatile addition to your home gym setup. Benefits of a Chin-Up Dip Station Chin-ups: Focus on your biceps, upper back, and forearms. Pull-ups: Engage your entire upper back, shoulders, and arms. Dips: Target your triceps, chest, and shoulders. Core Workouts: You can also incorporate hanging leg raises or knee raises for your abs. How to Use a Chin-Up Dip Station 1. Chin-Ups Chin-ups are done with an underhand grip (palms facing you), which focuses more on the biceps and lower back. Steps: Grab the home gym chin up dip station with your palms facing towards you and your hands shoulder-width apart. Hang down with your arms fully extended and your legs slightly bent to avoid swinging. Pull yourself up toward the bar, leading with your chest, until your chin goes above the bar. Slowly lower your body back down to the starting position. Tips: Engage your core and avoid swinging your legs. Try to pull with your elbows rather than just relying on your arms. If you're a beginner, use resistance bands or perform assisted chin-ups. 2. Pull-Ups A pull-up is performed with an overhand grip (palms facing away from you) and is great for building back strength. Steps: Grip the home gym chin up dip station with your hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing away from you. Hang with your arms fully extended, keeping your core tight. Pull your chest toward the bar, keeping your shoulders engaged. Lower yourself back down to the starting position. Tips: Avoid using momentum; move controlled. Perform with a neutral spine and engage your back muscles, not just your arms. 3. Dips Dips primarily work the triceps, chest, and shoulders. You can adjust the intensity based on your body angle. Steps: Position yourself on the dip bars with your arms straight and your feet off the ground. Slowly lower your body by bending your elbows at a 90-degree angle while leaning slightly forward for chest engagement or staying upright for triceps focus. Tips: Keep your shoulders down and avoid shrugging during the dip. For a chest focus, lean slightly forward as you lower yourself. For triceps, keep your torso upright during the movement. 4. Core Exercises (Hanging Leg/Knee Raises) Using the home gym chin up dip station, you can also perform various core exercises like leg or knee raises. Steps: Hang from the chin-up bar with a firm grip. Keep your legs straight or slightly bent, and raise them up towards your chest. Lower your legs slowly back down to the starting position without swinging. Tips: Perform the exercise slowly to engage the core muscles properly. Focus on using your abs to lift your legs, not your momentum.", "images": []}

This would create a split bathroom with a sink and a space for my makeup vanity, while leaving the original bathroom untouched. We would then install 24\" deep, floor-to-ceiling wardrobes along the shared wall, giving us 11' of closet space and providing some acoustic insulation between the bedroom and the bathroom. Option 2: In this option, we would move the entry to the bathroom from the nook to the bedroom, using a pocket door. title: How to interpret wide price range between electrical quotes? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "michael-macemon", "author_name": "Michael Macemon", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/michael-macemon", "date": "2025-02-15", "text": "We have a 1950s house in Eugene, OR that has an original Zinsco breaker panel along with several 1960s-era sub-panels. I understand these are fire risks and should be replaced. Additionally, we have plans for an addition to the house that will require re-locating the electrical meter and masthead (but the breaker panels can stay in their current location). I've had quotes from 2 electricians so far to move the meter and replace the panel. One was ~$6000, and the other was ~$14,500! Asking around, I've been told by others (albeit not electricians) that this should be a $1500-$3000 job. No new electrical work - this is just to eliminate the fire risk and clear the masthead and meter away from where we hope to do future work. I'm shocked by both quotes, and want to check with reality. Should I keep looking for someone who will do it for half as much as the lower quote or is that just wishful thinking?", "images": []}

title: Are these test results meaningful? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "central-valley", "author_name": "central_valley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/central-valley", "date": "2025-02-18", "text": "I'm testing my soil for pH and NPK for the first time, and I'm not sure what to make of the results I'm getting. Suggestions are welcome. I'm using an Environmental Concepts testing kit that I bought on Amazon a few months ago. Until today it was unopened. I'm testing five samples: The pH of all five samples came out to be 7.0 or 7.5. I don't know if those numbers are accurate, but they seem within reason. But the nitrogen content of all five samples came out to be 0. I'm suspicious of that. I just don't see how a mixture of leaf mold and chicken droppings, with a few wood shavings mixed in, can contain no nitrogen. And being suspicious of that nitrogen result makes me suspicious of the other four. I have not performed the phosphorus and potassium tests yet. I\u2019m waiting to read the comments on this post before I decide whether it\u2019s worth the effort. The kit has no expiration date, but should be reasonably new. The instructions are somewhat complex but easy to understand, and I followed them carefully. Unless I read the instructions five times and misunderstood them the same way each time, I don't see how my technique could have been at fault. Should I accept these results as valid? Buy a better test kit (if so, what)? Or just forget about home testing and send my soil out for analysis?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2025-02-18", "text": "I'm not sure what sources you have been investigating but the costs you quote are extraordinarily high. Germination (I am assured) takes place after 5-8 days! This sounded highly dubious to me. I have grown numerous varieties of poppy, with varying degrees of success.  Afaics, just about all of them require a certain amount of vernalisation...with alpines and hardy types such as p.nudicaule most definitely so. But ya know...they were an eye-watering price and the advice came straight from the Italian breeders. Snapdragons, I admit to being a total novice.  3 weeks later, there is not a sniff of a single seed and I am doubting my own ability. TBF, I bought them from a company which sends out lush catalogues which have pulled me in, numerous times...but  resulted in  woeful germination over many attempts and several years, I have avoided them for the last decade...but greed and lust overcame my generally cheapskate nature, as they are the sole outlet in the entire UK (for retail). I am now completely flustered...wondering what to do with the seed tray (around 50 of each variety). title: 36" cooktop or 30" rangetop? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kws578", "author_name": "KWS", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kws578", "date": "2025-02-19", "text": "We're finally getting around to our kitchen remodel. In our last house, we had a 36\" Wolf range, and loved it but rarely needed all the burners. I would love some feedback here! My main issue to solve is pan crowding. We have a cruddy 30\" GE gas cooktop, and both width wise and depth wise, I have issues with using multiple large pans. It's basically like a 24\" cooktop since the controls are on the side. We also want wall ovens, as we don't want to bend over to access the range oven (back issues). For this house, I was set on a 36\" Wolf gas cooktop, but am concerned that there would be pan crowding issues after seeing them in a showroom yesterday. It really doesn't give amymore space than what we have now. Basically, you get that one extra burner on the back behind the controls. And you still have the depth issue potentially. In our lake house, we have a 30\" range that has 5 burners, and I find it to have plenty of space for my large pans. The middle burner isn't really all that functional unless we use the integrated griddle pan on it, but I don't have crowding issues. So I got to thinking, would we be better off with a 30\" rangetop? title: Love this old school cabinet maker, but his contract process is loose | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-40364943", "author_name": "Jeanette Mieko", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-40364943", "date": "2025-02-21", "text": "UPDATE at the bottom, got lots of good advice and I'm better resourced. Just letting you know, in case you have tips that reading the update might relieve you of worrying about me going off track  :) Original post: I'm subbing out the work, No GC. I found a cabinet maker!  I've seen good work by him and he's a super nice, local guy with a small shop. He is making the boxes and ordering the faces. He didn't provide a written estimate or refer to a contract. He has texted estimates.  Maybe he is planning to provide a contract when I give him the full-on go ahead. However, he wanted me to sign off on his drawings, which are not that specific. See below. All the marker marks are mine. To be fair, it's not his job to design my kitchen. On my end, I did not provide  CAD drawings and I don't have a kitchen designer. I may need to change that. So NOW, I am writing up a Scope of Work listing all the cabinet doors and drawers with sizes, specifying the deets. Do I  expect documentation from the cabinet millworks for the 1 year warranty they provide? The cabinet maker says he, himself, does not provide a warranty. Final question, do you ask for a sample of the cabinet from the cabinet company as part of the agreement? Sign off on the sample in some way? Or just the description? I don't have red flags about the guy. I just saw him at his shop and he is making some nice, tight cabinet boxes.  However, he has an old school handshake way of working with limited documentation and no digital interface (except by text).", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4702b11407b80228_2461-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/70c2b69e07b8022c_2461-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4fb2ad6c07b8022e_2462-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1862368112", "author_name": "The Kitchen Place", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1862368112", "date": "2025-02-21", "text": "One of the biggest issues we see here on this forum, is lack of communication between cabinet designer/seller and the homeowner. But I also speculate that this cabinetmaker probably isn't charging you a fee for design and estimate time.  So he's probably throwing out a ballpark price and waiting for you to commit (with a deposit) before going into the nitty gritty details.  If he has the right number of cabinets to fill the space, the right wood specie/finish/hinges/guides, the right accessories you want and the right amount of moldings you need, that should be a REALLY good ballpark figure for you to decide to order or not.  Tweaking a design usually doesn't alter the price that much. To answer your questions. 1.  Yes, have a detailed cabinet list and elevations with cabinet SKU's, custom modifications and any jobsite/installation notes.  Include the Doorstyle, wood and finish, sizes of each cabinet and any accessories on the interior. Specify any finished interior cabinets, finished ends, routed for glass doors, custom modifications, linear amounts of moldings needed (scribe, shoe, crown, flat stock, toekick)....etc. 2.  Yes, get a payment schedule...but realize that change orders are due immediately. 3.  Yes, provide drawings for him.  It will help see what you want.  He's not a mind-reader.  Communicate everything.  Although there are probably some things you don't know. 4. A final set of drawings should be provided with all the details. You and he should go over it and each initial the page....copies made for both of you. 5.  Why would you need a breakdown on labor?  You can ask him if he can do that.  But if he's making them, he should install them.  If he gives you a labor/materials break down....yes you can get your own installer....but the savings could bite you in the you know what.  People that do that to save money (and I get why they do.)....but it only causes problems and finger pointing.  Always best to the company install that's supplying the cabinetry. 6.  If your door and drawer fronts are being ordered from another company...then YES absolutely specify the company name etc.  (ie.  Connestoga, Lancaster Door, Slab Drawer, Maple wood, unfinished) Hope this helps, Kelly ps.  I noticed your ref. end panels are only 24\" deep...check the specs on your refrigerator. One common complaint is the black box of the fridge sticks out and is ugly.  I almost always specify 27\", 30\" or 33\" end panels.  They can always be trimmed down on site if needed.  I like to cover the BOX of the fridge completely...and have the doors proud of the box and end panels. -Also beware of tall pantries next to refrigerators or oven cabinets.  If the door of the pantry swings INTO the refrigerator handle...it could damage the cabinet door. Try to swing away from it. And on the flip side, if your ref. door swings into the cabinet handle, it can DENT your REF. -One other piece of advice...make sure there's fillers included against side walls. -A good place for tray storage is over the refrigerator -Be sure to give him spec sheets on ALL of your appliances", "images": []}}

Does it mean it's not used, or is it meant to soak-in water from paving?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/936226df07b841cd_8721-w500-h223-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/22223cd107b841cf_8722-w500-h223-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

The home looks new and maybe the brick paver tradespeople were not doing there job correctly.    This should not be full of sand to the top, it should be like the other overflow relief gully.  No blockages.   Depending on what type of overflow, it may not have an internal pipe, but needs to be clear of any blockages.      It\u2019s been along time in WA since we had a lot of rain. title: Integrating Health Coaching with Telemedicine A Holistic Approach to | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "frederick-smith53", "author_name": "Frederick Smith", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/frederick-smith53", "date": "2025-02-21", "text": "The healthcare landscape is evolving at an unprecedented rate, with technological advancements reshaping how we access care, monitor health, and maintain overall well-being. One of the most promising developments in this transformation is the integration of health coaching with telemedicine. As healthcare continues to become more patient-centered and digital-first, combining these two approaches can result in more personalized, accessible, and effective care. The Rise of Telemedicine Telemedicine has gained significant traction over the past few years, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. With social distancing mandates and the rise of telehealth platforms, patients began to embrace virtual consultations with their healthcare providers. Telemedicine allows individuals to access medical advice, diagnoses, prescriptions, and follow-up care remotely, significantly reducing the barriers of distance, time, and convenience. But the potential of telemedicine extends beyond just traditional medical consultations. Increasingly, patients are looking for comprehensive, holistic care that goes beyond symptom management and addresses the root causes of health issues, such as lifestyle choices, stress, nutrition, and exercise habits. This is where health coaching comes in. What is Health Coaching? Health coaching is a collaborative process in which a trained professional supports individuals in making sustainable lifestyle changes. Health coaches focus on areas such as nutrition, physical activity, stress management, sleep hygiene, and emotional well-being. They serve as guides, helping individuals set goals, overcome obstacles, and develop habits that lead to long-term health improvements. While health coaches do not diagnose or treat medical conditions, they play a critical role in supporting overall wellness and preventing chronic diseases. Their work complements medical care by helping patients adopt healthier habits that contribute to improved outcomes and a better quality of life. Synergy Between Health Coaching and Telemedicine The integration of health coaching into telemedicine represents a natural evolution of patient care. By combining virtual medical consultations with coaching, patients can receive a more comprehensive and continuous form of care that addresses both their immediate health needs and long-term lifestyle changes. Telemedicine often provides patients with the ability to consult with medical professionals remotely for conditions like acute illnesses, follow-up appointments, or chronic disease management. However, it is typically more focused on diagnosing and treating symptoms. Health coaching, on the other hand, emphasizes a holistic approach to health and well-being, which includes diet, exercise, mental health, and behavior change. By integrating the two, patients can receive both medical treatment and personalized coaching to improve their overall health. For example, a patient who is managing type 2 diabetes might have a telemedicine consultation with a doctor to adjust their medication. Following the consultation, they could engage in health coaching to learn how to make lifestyle changes, such as adopting a balanced diet and increasing physical activity, which would support their long-term health goals. This combination offers a more well-rounded treatment plan that addresses the root causes of chronic conditions, rather than just managing their symptoms. One of the biggest barriers to traditional health coaching is accessibility. In-person coaching sessions can be time-consuming and may not be available in all areas, especially for individuals in rural or underserved communities. Telemedicine, however, removes these geographical barriers, enabling patients to access health coaching from the comfort of their homes. Health coaches who integrate with telemedicine platforms can offer virtual consultations through video calls, phone calls, or even messaging, making it easier for individuals to access coaching services regardless of their location. This is especially beneficial for people who may not have the time or resources to attend in-person sessions, such as busy professionals or those with mobility issues. Telemedicine platforms often come with built-in tools for remote monitoring of vital signs, such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose levels, and even sleep patterns. These tools provide valuable data that can be shared with health coaches to inform their guidance and recommendations. By tracking a patient\u2019s health metrics over time, health coaches can offer tailored advice that aligns with the patient\u2019s progress, adjusting their recommendations based on real-time data.", "images": []}

Since we will be breaking some of the concrete near garage door area, so we thought that might as well to replace the sewer lateral (which is also outside garage). Then we thought, since we will be replacing the sewer lateral and it's a smaller ~1460 sqft house with just one level, we might as well \"also\" replace the pluming of the entire house (as we will be replacing all the electrical wires in the house). Here are my questions: 1. Is such thinking logical? We want to control our budget, and we want to make sure that every penny spent would make sense. The kitchen will also be remodeled, but currently there is nothing wrong with the kitchen plumbing (as far as I know), and we will not change the location of kitchen sinks, etc. However, the house is old (1937), and who knows what can happen with the current old plumbing. The thing is that by investing so much $$$ to replace the plumbing of the entire house, it may (or may not) increase the value of the house. It seems that we are just paying for a \"peace of mind\". What are your opinions to replace the plumbing of the entire house? Would you do it? Why and why not? 2. Is there any big advancement (or innovation) regarding single family home plumbing, for the past 88 years? I don't know if the plumbing had been changed for this 1937 house before (no city records). title: Do you do hop water?  Or other flavored sparkling water? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "plllog", "author_name": "plllog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/plllog", "date": "2025-02-21", "text": "I'm not a beer drinker.  I do braise with it.  I don't hate it, but rarely have occasion, and even if I do, it's more likely to be a wheat ale or dark ale than a true beer.  Apparently, hop water (hops flavored \"sparkling water\" (generally with a beer-like big head of foam)) is being touted for a beer flavor for people who aren't in a position to be drinking actual beer. Not me!  But my \"vice\" is caffeine free Diet Coke.  Not much of it, but I say, \"All the chemicals, none of the nutrition.\"  Over ice, with a straw, it's a very soothing application when I have a sore throat and eustachian tubes (allergies). Turns out hop water works just as well!  It's equally 0 calories, and the right kind of cold and soothing. The one I particularly like is Hoplark Citra Hops.  It's very floral and nicely sweet tasting, with a sour/bitter finish that reminds me of the beer my father used to drink.  It's kind of weird, but nice, and I like that it's just hops and water. and citric acid. I've tried their sabro hops version, which is supposed to taste tropical but I get bitter water with a sour finish.  Not bad, per se, but nothing to seek out. I also tried a new, organic, fruit fizzy, but ... EWW ... The hops water slightly bitter finish that reminds me of Daddy's beer he'd give me a sip of when I was small enough to sit on his knee is a good thing.  \"Fruit\" flavored soda water flavor which also evokes early childhood by tasting like Play-Doh?  Heck, no!!  No, no, no!!!  I don't care if it's \"organic\" and \"natural\" in origin.  It tastes like non-food chemicals!  Sad ones. Do you like hop water? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~564423447", "author_name": "The KEEPING ROOM", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~564423447", "date": "2025-02-23", "text": "Before I retired and closed my store, I sold lots of leather reclining sofas and sectionals. Are you looking to change the colors, or do you need the space to function differently?  If so, exactly how? Without that information, here are my stabs-in-the-dark: I\u2019d remove the storage over the toilet in favor of art. I was going to make this recommendation. This way.....if for whatever reason the 1st flush produces a weak stem, I still have plenty of ~material~ to recut back on the long stem Am I approaching this theory wrong.... I just did this on my Semi Established Munstead one. I cut all the orignal stems on it , which was thin and weak.   1. Turn off the electricity
  2. Remove the cover plate and outlet from the old electrical box.
  3. Look inside the box to find where the electrical box is attached to the stud, where the electrical cable enters the box, and the height of the box from the floor.
  4. In the closet, determine where to put the new electrical box considering that it must be on the same side of the stud as the old box, must not interfere with the old electrical cable, and should (probably) be the same height from the floor as the existing box.
  5. Remove a knockout from the side of the old box that will face the new box.
  6. Buy an old work electrical box and cut a hole for it.
  7. Run a piece of 14/2 Romex (electrical cable) from the old box's knockout to the new box and clamp it to both boxes.
  8. To the outlet in the old box, reattach the old and new electrical cables.
  9. To an outlet in the new box, attach the new electrical cable.
  10. Attach the cover plates.
  11. Turn on the electricity.
  12. Grab the dog and run out the door so you don't die in the fire.

title: Documentary of Consumerism, intentional waste and profit | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2025-02-26", "text": "We are watching Buy Now! on Netflix. People formerly from within the industry, and some currently in industries discuss how consumers are manipulated into constantly buying new products, how intentional obsolescence has advanced, and how intentionally destroying brand new products increases profits. Salient points. A manufacturer who makes the majority of the dress shirts produced in the industry (across many retailers at multiple price points discusses how when he started in the industry there were essentially two clothing seasons, and most large retailers introduced maybe 1000 total new products  in a line two times a year.  Now some retailers introduce new clothing lines every month, even every two weeks. Schein introduces between 2000 and 10,000 new products daily. Jeff B's company, a former employee, said she was responsible back near the beginning working on convincing consumer that it was safe and enjoyable to buy any sort of product, and she said at first she really felt that she was making things convenient and provided access to people who did not have varied access. Just as an aside, she said JB thought nothing of saying to upper level employees: \"You are stupid, you should not be talking right now\".\" The problem came to a head when she realized how many brand new products were being disposed of regularly--I think all returns are essentially destroyed, but brand new products that never leave their warehouses are destroyed. There was footage of brand new merchandize with  holes cut in it or smashed  so no one could trash pick it. In the food industry, brand new, unexpired seasonal food, like halloween candy, christmas candy, valentine's candy, easter candy, all  identical except for wrapping, is thrown away by the ton. When one chain of prepared packaged  food discovered that people were taking the food from the dumpster (because it is disposed of Before it is expired), employees are ordered to open all the packages, mix the food together and then dump old coffee grounds and garbage on it. A chain of hot food items disposes of their food by mixing it all together in a big vat so that it is inedible, and then they have to weigh it to calculate waste. And there are cameras on them to make sure they aren't stealing the things that are going to be thrown out anyway. A former Bed Bath and Bodyworks employee said that they found out people were dumpster diving their regularly disposed of, unexpired, unsold product and that the \"solution\" was to pour it all out together because \"We don't want Bed Bath and Bodyworks to be associated with the brand that homeless people use.\" Almost all small electronics are engineered to stop working after a certain amount of time regardless of actual used. Most of them are made so that the battery cannot be changed. Phones used to be screwed together until they determined that people were changing batteries. Then they started using those screws that are hard to unscrew. Now many phones are glued together. The man who started IFixIt (?) gets cease and desist letters all the time for fixing phones and ipads and tablets and so forth. An industry specialist says \"They need to protect the integrity of our brand, he should not be altering them.\" He says \"They are broken, the customer knows they broke it themselves.\"", "images": []}

I have a very specific roadmap that I follow to select a whole home color palette. Step one - decide what must stay  (don't want to change, can't afford to change).   In your case it may be the flooring, furniture and kitchen cabinets , countertops, art in the entry.   You have to tell us what must stay.  If you only want to work with updating wall colors and don't want to paint trim it is fine, we just need to keep the black trim in mind while working through the process. Step two - determine your signature colors - those colors that draw you to them and make you buy things.   Colors that make your heart sing.    Walking through a home I will often notice that someone has the same 2 or 3 colors represented over and over in decorative items they have purchased and in their closets.  For me it is purple and teal and wine reds.  My sister is fall colors, greens and golds and orange reds.   My sister in law has tons of cornflower blues and peach and cream.   Step 3 - Determine the neutral color family that will work with what must stay and the colors that you love.     In most cases the walls will act as a backdrop for our art and furnishings, not the main focus.    There are some exceptions, like some Victorian homes, where the wall coverings can be the focus. Neutral color families include: Pink beige, orange beige, yellow beige, green beige, greige (green gray beige), green gray, blue gray, violet gray and taupe (purple/pink gray beige). My colors look best with taupe and violet gray.   My sister's look best with green undertones (green grays, greige and green beige and can work with yellow beige. My sister in law's colors work with the neutrals from yellow beige through blue gray - no orange, pink or purple undertones. Step 4 - Decide how  to use the colors that you love and neutrals throughout the home. General rule of thumb is to use the neutral through the main public areas of the house - Entry, living room, family room, hallways.   Add colors or use continue with the neutral in the bedrooms, bathrooms, laundry room . . .   You have to figure out where there are architectural breaks that make color change possible.   For each room you want to think about how the colors are going to flow from room to room to make the whole home feel harmonious. 2 examples: The accent colors in the main living area are used in the bedrooms and bathrooms to tie everything together.  The dining room has both the greens from the living room and the purples from the bedroom.  For my own home I started with the entry and painted the walls my chosen neutral.
